music.title: Listen to Orville Peck’s New Song “Too Little, Too Late”
music.summary: Emmylou Harris, Noah Cyrus, and Allison Russell feature on the singer's second LP, due out September 18
music.body:
Emmylou Harris, Noah Cyrus, and Allison Russell feature on the singer's second LP, due out September 18.

The guest list is the most informative part of that sentence. Emmylou Harris has spent fifty years functioning as country music's credential — an appearance from her is how the genre's establishment signals that an outsider is being taken seriously, and she has done it before for artists Nashville was not sure about. Allison Russell arrives from a different direction, with roots in Montreal, a background in folk and blues, and a body of work that has pushed hard against who country is understood to be for.

Peck's whole project sits on that fault line. A masked singer working in classic honky-tonk arrangements, openly gay, borrowing from an era of country that was not built to include him — the fringe is a costume and also an argument about who the tradition belongs to. The music itself is rarely ironic, which is what keeps it from being a bit.

That combination is why the record matters more than a single release usually would. A September album date means the campaign has to hold attention for months, and the collaborators are doing the work of saying, early, that this is a country record rather than a country-adjacent one.

music.title: U2 and DJ Martin Garrix Unveil New Single “Fireflies”: Stream
music.summary: Members of the Irish band, which is gearing up for an album drop later this year, and the Dutch DJ have collaborated in the past
music.body:
Members of the Irish band, which is gearing up for an album drop later this year, and the Dutch DJ have collaborated in the past.

The pairing is less unlikely than it looks. U2 have been reaching toward dance production since the early nineties, when Achtung Baby and Zooropa deliberately dismantled the earnest arena sound they had spent a decade building. That record was made in Berlin during reunification, with Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois pushing them toward loops, distortion, and irony, and it remains the clearest example in rock of a huge band choosing to alienate part of its audience on purpose.

What has changed is the direction of the borrowing. In 1991 a rock band adopting electronic production was slumming, at least in the press. Now the EDM producer is the one with the larger streaming audience, and the collaboration reads as a legacy act renting relevance — which is a fair criticism and also exactly the kind of trade that has kept U2 commercially viable for forty-five years.

The useful question for a station is narrower than the culture-war framing. Does the record work in a sequence? Big-room dance production and a stadium rock vocal are both built for enormous spaces, and songs designed for a room of eighty thousand people frequently sound thin coming out of a kitchen speaker.

music.title: Johnny Depp Is Basically Jack Sparrow as Scrooge in Trailer for Ebenezer: Watch
music.summary: The film marks Depp's first major studio project since his lengthy legal battle with Amber Heard.
music.body:
The film marks Depp's first major studio project since his lengthy legal battle with Amber Heard.

The reason a music page carries a film trailer is that screen placement is now one of the most powerful forces in the music business. A single well-chosen needle drop can return a decades-old record to the charts in a matter of days, and the effect is large enough that sync licensing has become a primary revenue line rather than a bonus — one of the arguments behind the wave of catalog acquisitions over the past several years.

A Christmas Carol adaptation is a specific case of this. Holiday music is the most reliably profitable catalog in existence, generating income every December in perpetuity, and a high-profile adaptation gives labels a reason to push both the score and whatever period or seasonal material gets licensed alongside it.

There is a second thing worth naming plainly. A studio casting decision of this kind is itself the news, because it is a public judgment about whether an actor's audience has come back. Studios make that call using the same logic labels use when deciding whether to work a record: not whether the person is admired, but whether enough people will still show up.

music.title: Charli XCX Gives Her Top 5 Underrated Films
music.summary: Sofia Coppola and David Lynch films made the pop singer's list.
music.body:
Sofia Coppola and David Lynch films made the pop singer's list.

A list like this is worth reading as source material rather than trivia. Charli XCX has spent a decade working at the seam between mainstream pop and the more abrasive electronic scene around PC Music — hyperpop, before that word became a marketing category — and the defining feature of that work is that the references are always visible. The production quotes rave, early-2000s club music, and industrial noise without hiding any of it.

Coppola and Lynch make sense in that context for opposite reasons. Coppola's films are largely about surface, mood, and the specific loneliness of being looked at, which is close to the emotional territory of a lot of Charli's writing. Lynch built a career on putting menace directly underneath something pretty, and he was unusually attentive to sound design — his collaborations with Angelo Badalamenti are still being borrowed from by producers who have never seen the films.

That is the value in an artist naming influences honestly. It gives a listener somewhere to go next, and it makes the records legible as choices rather than instincts. Pop artists have historically been discouraged from doing this, on the theory that visible influence undermines the illusion. The opposite is usually true.

music.title: Conor Oberst Says He’s Finding It “Almost Impossible” To Write About Trump Era
music.summary: "You can’t satirize, or whatever, what’s already like a parody," the Bright Eyes frontman said.
music.body:
"You can’t satirize, or whatever, what’s already like a parody," the Bright Eyes frontman said.

Oberst is describing an old problem in a new form. Protest songwriting has always depended on saying something the audience had not already heard stated more bluntly on the news, and the form works best when it supplies emotion the reporting cannot. When the subject is already absurd on its face, satire has nothing left to add — the joke has been made by the event.

The songs that survived earlier political moments mostly solved this by going small. The most durable protest music tends to work through a specific person in a specific situation rather than through argument, because an argument dates the moment its occasion passes and a person does not. Marvin Gaye's What's Going On is the canonical example, and its power comes from the fact that it asks rather than accuses.

Oberst's own catalog has done this before, with mixed results, and he is unusually candid about which attempts failed. That candor is the interesting part of the quote. An artist saying out loud that they cannot currently write about something is more useful than another record that tries and does not land — and it is a much harder thing to say in public.

chart.title: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' holds No. 1 for a 14th week
chart.summary: The country crossover keeps its long grip on the top of the Billboard Hot 100 — one of the year's longest runs.
chart.body:
Ella Langley isn't giving up the top spot. 'Choosin' Texas' holds at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 for a 14th week as of the July 25 chart — one of the longest runs of 2026 and a milestone for a country crossover.

Extended reigns like this have become rare in a streaming era of fast turnover, and the reason is structural. The Hot 100 blends streaming, radio airplay, and sales, and streaming is front-loaded by design: release-week mobilization produces enormous first-week numbers that decay quickly. Records that hold for months are almost always doing it on the radio side, where a song accumulates audience slowly and keeps it.

Country crossovers are especially good at this because country radio has longer song lifecycles than pop radio does. A record can spend six months climbing the country airplay chart, and when it crosses to pop it arrives with an established audience rather than a launch. That is the opposite of how most number ones now behave.

What it means practically is that the song has settled into everyday rotation — cars, cookouts, group chats — which is a different and far more durable condition than being the biggest release of a given week. Fourteen weeks is not a marketing outcome. It is people choosing it repeatedly.

chart.title: Olivia Dean lands two songs in the Hot 100's top 10
chart.summary: 'Man I Need' and 'So Easy' both sit inside the top 10 as the London singer's breakout accelerates.
chart.body:
Olivia Dean is having the kind of summer that turns a rising name into a household one. This week she holds two songs inside the Billboard Hot 100's top 10 — 'Man I Need' and 'So Easy' — a rare double for an artist still early in her American breakthrough.

Two simultaneous top 10s is a meaningfully different signal from one. A single hit can be produced by a playlist placement or a sync; two at once usually means the audience has moved from liking a song to following an artist, which is the transition most careers never make. It is also the point at which radio programmers start treating a name as a known quantity rather than a risk.

Dean's route there is worth noting because it is unfashionable. Warm, soul-inflected pop with live-feeling arrangements, built through touring and word of mouth over several years rather than a viral spike. That path is slower and it produces a more durable base — audiences who found an artist through repeated live exposure behave very differently from audiences delivered by an algorithm.

For a station, records like these are structurally useful. They are melodically direct enough to sit in daytime rotation and textured enough not to wear out, which is a narrower overlap than it sounds.

chart.title: Taylor Swift stays near the top of the Hot 100
chart.summary: Swift holds a spot high in the top 10 this week, a reliable fixture on the singles chart.
chart.body:
Taylor Swift remains a fixture near the summit of the Billboard Hot 100, holding a place high in the top 10 on the July 25 chart.

What makes her chart behavior distinctive is not the peaks but the floor. Most artists at this scale post enormous debuts and then fall out of the top tier within a few weeks, because the audience that mobilized on release day has already streamed the record. Swift's catalog instead maintains a persistent baseline across dozens of songs at once, which is closer to how a radio format behaves than how a single artist usually does.

A large part of that is deliberate infrastructure. The re-recorded albums restored control over her masters and, incidentally, doubled the amount of chart-eligible Swift catalog in circulation. Combined with an audience that treats new releases as events, the effect is that she competes with her own back catalog for chart positions — a problem almost nobody else has.

For a summer crowded with country crossovers and pop returns, that constancy is its own kind of data point. Records come and go from the top of the chart on the strength of a moment. Staying there through several of those moments is a different achievement, and it is the one that keeps a catalog in heavy rotation long after the campaign ends.

ditmas.title: Two-alarm fire burns vacant Flatbush home long slated for redevelopment
ditmas.summary: A two-alarm fire burned through a long-vacant Flatbush building on Saturday morning at 1952 Nostrand Ave.
ditmas.body:
A two-alarm fire burned through a long-vacant Flatbush building on Saturday morning. Firefighters arrived at 1952 Nostrand Ave. just after 6:40 a.m. on July 18 to find the three-story wood-framed home enveloped in thick smoke. The blaze had begun in the building’s basement, per the FDNY, and spread up to the first floor.

The phrase doing the most work in that report is wood-framed. Much of this part of Brooklyn was built between the 1890s and the 1920s as detached and semi-detached wooden houses, a construction type that is now rare in New York and largely prohibited at this scale under current fire codes. It is the reason the streets look the way they do, and it is also why a basement fire in one of these buildings escalates quickly — the framing itself is the fuel path.

Long-vacant is the other detail worth pausing on. Buildings held empty pending redevelopment accumulate risk in predictable ways: no active utilities to monitor, no occupants to report a problem early, and frequently unsecured access. Fires in vacant structures are disproportionately represented in FDNY responses for exactly these reasons.

Which makes this a housing story as much as an incident report. A wood-frame house standing empty on a commercial avenue is a decision someone made, and the fire is one of the ways that decision eventually becomes everyone's problem.

ditmas.title: Back-to-back Bed-Stuy blazes among series of weekend Brooklyn blazes
ditmas.summary: Fire marshals are investigating multiple Brooklyn fires that broke out over the weekend, including back-to-back blazes in Bedford-Stuyvesant.
ditmas.body:
Fire marshals are investigating multiple Brooklyn fires that broke out over the weekend, including back-to-back blazes in Bedford-Stuyvesant on Saturday. Firefighters first responded just after 12:45 p.m. to an apartment fire at 210 Stuyvesant Ave. near Gates Avenue. Units from the 57th Battalion arrived to find fire in an apartment.

Bed-Stuy's building stock is a large part of the context. The neighborhood holds one of the densest concentrations of nineteenth-century brownstones and row houses in the country, much of it built between the 1870s and the 1900s. Attached row construction means a fire has a shared wall and a shared cockloft — the void beneath the roof running across multiple buildings — which is the classic path by which a single apartment fire becomes a multi-building response.

That is why the department's staffing on these calls looks disproportionate to a civilian. A row-house fire is treated as a potential block fire from the moment it is reported, and the first-arriving units are checking neighboring buildings before the original one is under control.

The preservation of that housing stock is one of the genuine achievements of Brooklyn's landmarking movement, and it comes with this permanent trade-off. The buildings are beautiful, they are irreplaceable at current construction costs, and they were designed before anyone was thinking about fire separation between one home and the next.

ditmas.title: New mosaics combine Flatbush’s theatrical history and vibrant culture at Church Avenue station
ditmas.summary: Lush mosaics by artist Christopher Myers marry the neighborhood’s theatrical history with the cultures of its present.
ditmas.body:
In a subway station that has served Flatbush for over a century, a series of lush mosaics marry the neighborhood’s theatrical history with the vibrant cultures of its present. The MTA and artist Christopher Myers unveiled the pieces at Church Avenue station.

The theatrical history being referenced is real and largely forgotten. Flatbush Avenue was a genuine entertainment corridor in the first half of the twentieth century, anchored by enormous movie palaces built when going to the pictures was a formal occasion — Kings Theatre, which opened in 1929 with around three thousand seats, is the surviving example, and it sat dark for nearly forty years before its 2015 restoration.

The program behind the mosaics is worth knowing about. MTA Arts & Design has commissioned permanent work in stations since 1985, and it is one of the largest public art programs in the country. The medium is deliberate: glass mosaic and faience were chosen because they survive a hundred years of hands, weather, and cleaning in a way that paint or print cannot.

What makes a station commission different from a gallery show is the audience. Nobody chooses to see it. Several thousand people a day walk past on their way to a train, most of them from the neighborhood depicted, and the work has to hold up under that kind of repeated, half-attentive looking. That is a harder brief than a wall in a museum.

brooklyn.title: Larger than life rock meets burlesque side show ‘Cherry Hellodies 7: South of Heaven’ coming to Coney Island
brooklyn.summary: A spectacular combining heavy metal, death-defying stunts and sideshow returns to Coney Island USA on Aug. 1.
brooklyn.body:
A one-of-a-kind spectacular that combines heavy metal, death-defying stunts and sideshow is returning to Coney Island. On Aug. 1 at 9 p.m., “Cherry Hellodies 7: South of Heaven” will make its way to the sideshow stage at Coney Island USA.

Current Coney Island sideshow exists because of a deliberate rescue. Coney Island USA was founded in 1980 by Dick Zigun, who set out to preserve a form that had essentially died out in America — the traditional ten-in-one sideshow, with fire eating, sword swallowing, and human blockhead acts performed live rather than as film footage. Sideshows by the Seashore is the last permanently housed one in the country, and the organization runs a school to keep the skills from disappearing entirely.

The metal pairing is less of a novelty than it sounds. Both traditions are built on spectacle, endurance, and a performer's willingness to do something the audience believes might genuinely go wrong, and both have spent decades being dismissed as low culture by people who had not watched closely.

Worth noting that the stunts are real. Sword swallowing is an actual physical skill with an actual injury rate, not an illusion, which is most of why the form survived at all. Nothing about the act works if the audience suspects a trick.

brooklyn.title: Things to do this weekend in NYC, July 24-26: Block parties, Pokémon, free ice cream and more!
brooklyn.summary: A look at some of the best events happening around town between July 24-26, including a vinyl take-back event at Rough Trade.
brooklyn.body:
There are plenty of great things to do around New York City this weekend. Here’s a look at some of the best events happening around town between July 24-26, including a Rough Trade NYC and WMG vinyl take-back event on Friday.

The vinyl take-back is the item worth pulling out, because it points at a real problem. Vinyl outsold CDs again this year, and the format's revival is now well over a decade old — but records are made of PVC, which is not meaningfully recyclable through municipal systems and which produces a substantial carbon footprint per unit. The industry has spent the past few years quietly acknowledging that the greenest format it sells is also its dirtiest per copy.

Take-back programs are a partial answer: collect unwanted records, resell what is playable, and route the rest toward reprocessing rather than landfill. It does not solve manufacturing, and nobody involved claims it does.

For a weekend list the practical filter is the same one this page always applies. Block parties and free events are joinable — no ticket, no start time you have to hit, no cost to leaving early — which is why they consistently outperform ticketed programming as things people actually end up doing. Distance matters more than the listing suggests, and from this part of Brooklyn most of these are a transfer away.
bodyParagraphs: There are plenty of great things to do around New York City this weekend. Here’s a look at some of the best events happening around town between July 24-26, including a Rough Trade NYC and WMG vinyl take-back event on Friday.

The vinyl take-back is the item worth pulling out, because it points at a real problem. Vinyl outsold CDs again this year, and the format's revival is now well over a decade old — but records are made of PVC, which is not meaningfully recyclable through municipal systems and which produces a substantial carbon footprint per unit. The industry has spent the past few years quietly acknowledging that the greenest format it sells is also its dirtiest per copy.

Take-back programs are a partial answer: collect unwanted records, resell what is playable, and route the rest toward reprocessing rather than landfill. It does not solve manufacturing, and nobody involved claims it does.

For a weekend list the practical filter is the same one this page always applies. Block parties and free events are joinable — no ticket, no start time you have to hit, no cost to leaving early — which is why they consistently outperform ticketed programming as things people actually end up doing. brooklyn.title: Transportation advocates urge Mamdani to release new Vision Zero plan, expand Sammy’s law
brooklyn.summary: Advocates unveiled data showing a rise in traffic deaths during the first half of 2026 while pressing for a new Vision Zero plan.
brooklyn.body:
Transportation advocates on Thursday urged Mayor Zohran Mamdani to release a new plan for Vision Zero, the city’s program to eliminate fatalities and serious injuries from traffic crashes, while unveiling new data showing a rise in traffic deaths during the first half of 2026. The advocates included Transportation Alternatives and Families for Safe Streets.

Vision Zero began in Sweden in the 1990s and arrived in New York in 2014. Its founding premise is unusual for traffic policy: that deaths on the road are a design failure rather than an accident, and that a street which kills people is a street that was built wrong. The first and most consequential New York change under it was lowering the default speed limit to 25 mph, because survival rates for a struck pedestrian fall sharply above roughly 20 to 30 mph.

Sammy's Law is the follow-on fight. Named for Sammy Cohen Eckstein, a twelve-year-old killed by a van near Prospect Park in 2013, it concerns the city's authority to set its own speed limits without going through Albany — a question of home rule as much as street design.

This lands close to home. Flatbush, Nostrand, and Church Avenues are among the wider, faster arterials in central Brooklyn, and arterials are where the overwhelming majority of serious crashes happen. The design of those specific streets is the policy.

brooklyn.title: Mamdani selects 18 former judges, law school professors, advocate attorneys to join group helping to pick new judges
brooklyn.summary: The mayor named 18 people to a panel tasked with recommending candidates for the city's next judicial appointments.
brooklyn.body:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani took a step toward fulfilling a campaign promise to demystify how city judges are appointed on Wednesday, announcing a group of 18 former judges, law school professors, Legal Aid attorneys, public defenders and youth, consumer and worker rights lawyers to join a group tasked with recommending the city’s next judges.

The mechanism matters more than it sounds. New York's mayor directly appoints judges to the Criminal Court and the Family Court — the two benches most New Yorkers will ever encounter — and does so from a list produced by an advisory committee. Who sits on that committee therefore shapes the bench for years, and the panels have historically been weighted toward prosecutors and large-firm litigators.

Seating public defenders and Legal Aid attorneys on the screening body is the substantive change here. It reflects an argument that has been running in criminal justice reform circles for a decade: that a judiciary drawn overwhelmingly from one side of the courtroom produces predictable outcomes, and that the fix is upstream of any individual case.

For Brooklyn this is not abstract. Housing court, family court, and criminal court decisions made at Adams Street and Jay Street affect an enormous number of households in this borough, and almost none of it is covered. The appointments process is where those outcomes get set, quietly, years before anyone sees a docket.
